html:
The trade, from around 1330, that brought cobalt ore from Persia to the potters of Jingdezhen in China, who used it to paint the first great blue and white porcelain.

Cobalt is one of the few colours that survives the very high heat needed to fire porcelain. Potters in Iraq and Iran had used it on earthenware for centuries. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty, when China and the Ilkhanate in Iran were ruled by branches of the same family, Muslim merchants brought a rich Persian cobalt to Jingdezhen. The Chinese called it "Muslim blue".

Much of the early ware went back west. Large dishes, made for shared meals in the Islamic world, were shipped across the Indian Ocean and overland to Iran, Turkey, India, East Africa and Egypt. The Safavid shrine at Ardabil and the Topkapı Palace in Istanbul hold famous collections.

Under the Ming blue and white became China's leading export. Potters copied it everywhere, from the Iznik tiles of Ottoman Turkey to Delft in Holland. A colour from Iran, on a Chinese body, made for Muslim tastes, became a global style.
sum: The trade, from around 1330, that brought cobalt ore from Persia to the potters of Jingdezhen in China, who used it to paint the first great blue and white porcelain.
